allow the stars a wide material action upon the bodily part of the man, producing heat and cold and their natural resultants in the physical constitution ; still does such action explain character, vocation and especially all that seems quite independent of material elements, a man taking to letters, to geometry, to gambling, and becoming an originator in any of these pursuits ? And can we imagine the stars, divine beings, bestowing wickedness ? And what of a doctrine that makes them wreak vengeance, as for a wrong, because they are in their decline or are being carried to a position beneath the earth — as if a decline from our point of view brought any change to themselves, as if they ever ceased to traverse the heavenly spheres and to make the same figure around the earth.

Nor may we think that these divine beings lose or gain in goodness as they see this one or another of the company in various aspects, and that in their happier position they are benignant to us and, less pleasantly situated, turn maleficent. We can but believe that their circuit is for the protection of the entirety of things while they furnish the incidental service of being letters on which the augur, acquainted with that alphabet, may look and read the future from their pattern — arriving at the thing signified by such analogies as that a soaring bird tells of some lofty event.

chapters.title: Against the one chain of causes
chapters.summary: Last, the one principle that strings all things together and accomplishes everything by seed-principles. It is close to the view that all comes from the soul of the whole, though it would grant us something. But it holds every necessity: with all the causes taken in, nothing can stop anything. Our impressions follow what went before, our impulses follow them, and "what is up to us" is only a name: we would be like animals, infants and madmen, and fire too has its impulses. Everyone sees this, and looks for other causes.

older.label: III.1, chapter 7
older.text:
It remains to notice the theory of the one Causing-Principle alleged to interweave everything with everything else, to make things into a chain, to determine the nature and condition of each phenomenon — a Principle which, acting through seminal (operatively productive) Reason-Forms — Logoi Spermatikoi — elaborates all that exists and happens.

The doctrine is close to that which makes the Soul of the Universe the source and cause of all condition and of all movement whether without or — supposing that we are allowed as individuals some little power towards personal act — within ourselves.

But it is the theory of the most rigid and universal Necessity : all the causative forces enter into the system, and so every several phenomenon rises necessarily ; where nothing escapes Destiny, nothing has power to check or to change. Such forces beating upon us, as it were, from one general cause leave us no resource but to go where they drive. All our ideas will be determined by a chain of previous causes ; our doings will be determined by those ideas ; personal action becomes a mere word. That we are the agents does not save our freedom when our action is prescribed by those causes ; we have precisely what belongs to everything that lives, to infants guided by blind impulses, to lunatics ; all these act ; why, even fire acts ; there is act in everything that follows the plan of its being, servilely.

No one that sees the implications of this theory can hesitate : unable to halt at such a determinant principle, we seek for other explanations of our action.

chapters.title: Soul, the other principle
chapters.summary: What cause leaves nothing uncaused, keeps order, lets us be something, and saves foretelling? Soul: not only the soul of the whole but each one's, a first cause, not born of seeds. Without a body it is master of itself and free; in a body it is ranked with other things, and the chances it meets lead much of what it does. The better soul masters more, the worse less: the worse gives way to the body's blend, and is humbled by poverty or made a tyrant by power; the good soul changes things rather than being changed.

older.label: III.1, chapter 8
older.text:
What can this other cause be ; one standing above those treated of ; one that leaves nothing causeless, that preserves sequence and order in the Universe and yet allows ourselves some reality and leaves room for prediction and augury ?

Soul : we must place at the crest of the world of beings, this other Principle, not merely the Soul of the Universe but, included in it, the Soul of the individual : this, no mean Principle, is needed to be the bond of union in the total of things, not, itself, a thing sprung like things from life-seeds, but a first-hand Cause, bodiless and therefore supreme over itself, free, beyond the reach of kosmic Cause : for, brought into body, it would not be unrestrictedly sovereign ; it would hold rank in a series.

Now the environment into which this independent principle enters, when it comes to this midpoint, will be largely led by secondary causes (or, by chance-causes) : there will therefore be a compromise ; the action of the Soul will be in part guided by this environment while in other matters it will be sovereign, leading the way where it will. The nobler Soul will have the greater power ; the poorer Soul, the lesser. A soul which defers to the bodily temperament cannot escape desire and rage and is abject in poverty, overbearing in wealth, arbitrary in power. The soul of nobler nature holds good against its surroundings ; it is more apt to change them than to be changed, so that often it improves the environment and, where it must make concession, at least keeps its innocence.

chapters.title: What is up to us
chapters.summary: What comes of choice and chance blended is necessary: given all the causes, all things happen. When the soul acts as moved from outside, blindly, or uses wrong impulses because it is worse of itself, the act is not voluntary. Only when it moves by its own reason, pure and unaffected, is the impulse up to us: our own work, from within, from the pure soul, not from a soul led astray by ignorance or beaten by desires.

older.label: III.1, chapter 9
older.text:
We admit, then, a Necessity in all that is brought about by this compromise between evil and accidental circumstance : what room was there for anything else than the thing that is ? Given all the causes, all must happen beyond aye or nay — that is, all the external and whatever may be due to the sidereal circuit — therefore when the Soul has been modified by outer forces and acts under that pressure so that what it does is no more than an unreflecting acceptance of stimulus, neither the act nor the state can be described as voluntary : so, too, when even from within itself, it falls at times below its best and ignores the true, the highest, laws of action.

But when our Soul holds to its Reason-Principle, to the guide, pure and detached and native to itself, only then can we speak of personal operation, of voluntary act. Things so done may truly be described as our doing, for they have no other source ; they are the issue of the unmingled Soul, a Principle that is a First, a leader, a sovereign not subject to the errors of ignorance, not to be overthrown by the tyranny of the desires which, where they can break in, drive and drag, so as to allow of no act of ours, but mere answer to stimulus.

chapters.title: The sum
chapters.summary: All things are signified and come to be by causes of two kinds: some by soul, some by the things around. Souls that act by right reason act of themselves; when hindered, they suffer more than they act. So the causes of not being wise lie elsewhere, and these acts may be called destiny's; but the best come from us, as we are when we are alone. The good do fine things, and it is up to them; the others, when they are let breathe, not taking their wisdom from elsewhere, but only not hindered.

older.label: III.1, chapter 10
older.text:
To sum the results of our argument : — All things and events are foreshown and brought into being by causes ; but the causation is of two Kinds ; there are results originating from the Soul and results due to other causes, those of the environment.

In the action of our Souls all that is done of their own motion in the light of sound reason is the Soul's work, while what is done where they are hindered from their own action is not so much done as suffered. Unwisdom, then, is not due to the Soul, and, in general — if we mean by Fate a compulsion outside ourselves — an act is fated when it is contrary to wisdom.

But all our best is of our own doing : such is our nature as long as we remain detached. The wise and good do perform acts ; their right action is the expression of their own power : in the others it comes in the breathing spaces when the passions are in abeyance ; but it is not that they draw this occasional wisdom from outside themselves ; simply, they are for the time being unhindered.

paragraphs.modern: Plotinus, the philosopher of our own time, seemed like a man ashamed to be in a body. Because of this frame of mind he could not bear to talk about his family, his parents or his homeland. He thought it so far beneath him to sit for a painter or a sculptor that, when Amelius asked him to allow a likeness of him to be made, he said: "Is it not enough to carry the image that nature has wrapped around us? Must I also agree to leave behind an image of the image, to last longer, as if it were one of the works worth looking at?"
paragraphs.greek: Πλωτῖνος ὁ καθ’ ἡμᾶς γεγονὼς φιλόσοφος ἐῴκει μὲν αἰσχυνομένῳ, ὅτι ἐν σώματι εἴη. ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς τοιαύτης διαθέσεως οὔτε περὶ τοῦ γένους αὐτοῦ διηγεῖσθαι ἠνείχετο οὔτε περὶ τῶν γονέων οὔτε περὶ τῆς πατρίδος. ζωγράφου δὲ ἀνασχέσθαι ἢ πλάστου τοσοῦτον ἀπηξίου, ὥστε καὶ λέγειν πρὸς Ἀμέλιον δεόμενον εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι ἐπιτρέψαι· οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ φέρειν, ὃ ἡ φύσις εἴδωλον ἡμῖν περιτέθεικεν; ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰδώλου εἴδωλον συγχωρεῖν αὐτὸν ἀξιοῦν πολυχρονιώτερον καταλιπεῖν ὡς δή τι τῶν ἀξιοθεάτων ἔργων.
notes: "An image of the image": Plato's Republic X (597e-598b) puts the painter's work third from the truth, the imitation of an appearance. For Plotinus the body is already an image (εἴδωλον) that nature has put around us.

paragraphs.modern: So, since he refused and would not sit for it, Amelius, who had a friend, Carterius, the best of the painters of that time, had him come in and attend the meetings (anyone who wished could come to the meetings), and trained him, by paying closer and closer attention, to take in more striking impressions from what he saw. Then, as Carterius drew the likeness from the image stored in his memory, and Amelius helped him correct the sketch towards a resemblance, Carterius' talent made a portrait of him very like him, without Plotinus knowing.
paragraphs.greek: ὅθεν ἀπαγορεύοντος καὶ καθεδεῖσθαι ἕνεκα τούτου ἀρνουμένου ἔχων φίλον ὁ Ἀμέλιος Καρτέριον τὸν ἄριστον τῶν τότε γεγονότων ζωγράφων εἰσιέναι καὶ ἀπαντᾶν εἰς τὰς συνουσίας ποιήσας· ἐξῆν γὰρ τῷ βουλομένῳ φοιτᾶν εἰς τὰς συνουσίας· τὰς ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾶν φαντασίας πληκτικωτέρας λαμβάνειν διὰ τῆς ἐπὶ πλέον προσοχῆς συνείθισεν. ἔπειτα γράφοντος ἐκ τοῦ τῇ μνήμῃ ἐναποκειμένου ἰνδάλματος τὸ εἴκασμα καὶ συνδιορθοῦντος εἰς ὁμοιότητα τὸ ἴχνος τοῦ Ἀμελίου εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι ἡ εὐφυΐα τοῦ Καρτερίου παρέσχεν ἀγνοοῦντος τοῦ Πλωτίνου ὁμοιοτάτην.

paragraphs.modern: He often suffered from a disease of the bowels, but he would not put up with an enema, saying that it was not fitting for an old man to undergo such treatments; nor would he take the antidotes made from wild beasts, saying that he did not accept food from the bodies even of tame animals. He kept away from the baths, and had himself rubbed down every day at home; but when the plague grew heavy and the men who rubbed him died, he gave up this treatment, and little by little the savage form of the throat disease took hold of him. While I was with him nothing of this kind showed itself yet; but after I had sailed away the illness grew so fierce, as our companion Eustochius, who stayed with him until his death, told me when I came back, that his voice lost its clearness and its ring as he grew hoarse, his sight was clouded, and his hands and feet were covered with sores. So, since his friends avoided meeting him, because he had the habit of greeting everyone mouth to mouth, he left the city and went to Campania, and stayed at the estate of Zethus, an old companion of his who had died. What he needed was provided from Zethus' estate, and brought from Minturnae, from Castricius' lands; for Castricius had his property at Minturnae.
paragraphs.greek: κοιλιακῇ δὲ νόσῳ πολλάκις καταπονούμενος οὔτε κλυστῆρος ἠνέσχετο, οὐκ εἶναι πρὸς τοῦ πρεσβύτου λέγων ὑπομένειν τὰς τοιαύτας θεραπείας, οὔτε τὰς θηριακὰς ἀντιδότους λαβεῖν ὑπέμεινε, μηδὲ τῶν ἡμέρων ζῴων τὰς ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τροφὰς προσίεσθαι λέγων. λουτροῦ δὲ ἀπεχόμενος καὶ τρίψεσι καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν χρώμενος ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας, ἐπειδὴ τοῦ λοιμοῦ ἐπιβρίσαντος συνέβη τοὺς τρίβοντας αὐτὸν ἀποθανεῖν, ἀμελήσας τῆς τοιαύτης θεραπείας κατ’ ὀλίγον τὴν τοῦ κυνάγχου ἀγριότητα κατασκευαζομένην ἔσχε. κἀμοῦ μὲν παρόντος οὐδέν πω τοιοῦτον ὑπεφαίνετο· ἀποπλεύσαντος δὲ εἰς τοσοῦτον ἠγριώθη τὸ πάθος, ὡς ἔλεγεν ἐπανελθόντι Εὐστόχιος ὁ ἑταῖρος ὁ καὶ παραμείνας αὐτῷ ἄχρι θανάτου, ὡς καὶ τῆς φωνῆς περιαιρεθῆναι τὸ τορὸν καὶ εὔηχον βραγχῶντος αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν ὄψιν συγχυθῆναι καὶ τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τοὺς πόδας ἑλκωθῆναι· ὅθεν ἐκτρεπομένων αὐτοῦ τὰς συναντήσεις τῶν φίλων διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ στόματος πάντας προσαγορεύειν ἔθος ἔχειν, τῆς μὲν πόλεως ἀπαλλάττεται, εἰς δὲ τὴν Καμπανίαν ἐλθὼν εἰς Ζήθου χωρίον ἑταίρου παλαιοῦ αὐτῷ γεγονότος καὶ τεθνηκότος κατάγεται. τὰ δ’ ἀναγκαῖα αὐτῷ ἔκ τε τῶν τοῦ Ζήθου ἐτελεῖτο καὶ ἐκ Μιντουρνῶν ἐκομίζετο ἐκ τῶν Καστρικίου· ἐν Μιντούρναις γὰρ ὁ Καστρίκιος τὰς κτήσεις εἶχε.

flags.taylor: in a short while he contracted malign diphtheria
flags.why: The Greek says "little by little" (κατ’ ὀλίγον) the disease grew on him, not "in a short while"; and its name is κυνάγχη ("dog-choke"), the ancient name for a severe inflammation of the throat. "Malign diphtheria" is a modern diagnosis put into Porphyry's mouth.

flags.taylor: addressing everyone by word of mouth
flags.why: The Greek ἀπὸ στόματος πάντας προσαγορεύειν is most naturally "greeting everyone mouth to mouth", with a kiss, which is why his friends, afraid of his sores, kept away; "by word of mouth" makes it speech.

notes: The "antidotes from wild beasts" (θηριακαὶ ἀντίδοτοι) are theriacs, compound remedies against poison made with the flesh of wild animals, above all of vipers. Porphyry himself wrote a book On abstinence from animal food.

paragraphs.modern: When he was about to die, as Eustochius told us, since Eustochius, who lived at Puteoli, was slow in coming to him, he said: "I am still waiting for you." And saying that he was trying to bring the divine in us back up to the divine in the All, as a snake passed under the bed on which he lay and slipped into a hole in the wall, he breathed his last. He was, as Eustochius said, sixty-six years old, and the second year of Claudius' reign was coming to its end. When he died I, Porphyry, happened to be staying at Lilybaeum, Amelius at Apamea in Syria, and Castricius in Rome; only Eustochius was there.
paragraphs.greek: μέλλων δὲ τελευτᾶν, ὡς ὁ Εὐστόχιος ἡμῖν διηγεῖτο, ἐπειδὴ ἐν Ποτιόλοις κατοικῶν ὁ Εὐστόχιος βραδέως πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀφίκετο, εἰπὼν ὅτι σὲ ἔτι περιμένω καὶ φήσας πειρᾶσθαι τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν θεῖον ἀνάγειν πρὸς τὸ ἐν τῷ παντὶ θεῖον, δράκοντος ὑπὸ τὴν κλίνην διελθόντος ἐν ᾗ κατέκειτο καὶ εἰς ὀπὴν ἐν τῷ τοίχῳ ὑπάρχουσαν ὑποδεδυκότος ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα ἔτη γεγονώς, ὡς ὁ Εὐστόχιος ἔλεγεν, ἓξ τε καὶ ἑξήκοντα, τοῦ δευτέρου ἔτους τῆς Κλαυδίου βασιλείας πληρουμένου. τελευτῶντι δὲ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ μὲν ὁ Πορφύριος ἐτύγχανον ἐν Λιλυβαίῳ διατρίβων, Ἀμέλιος δὲ ἐν Ἀπαμείᾳ τῆς Συρίας, Καστρίκιος δὲ ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ· μόνος δὲ παρῆν ὁ Εὐστόχιος.
notes: The last words are read differently in the manuscripts and by modern editors: some read them as Plotinus' charge to those present ("try to bring back..."), some read "the god in us" for "the divine in us". The modern version keeps Volkmann's text: "saying that he was trying" (φήσας πειρᾶσθαι).
The second year of the emperor Claudius (Claudius II) is AD 270, in the modern reckoning.

paragraphs.modern: Counting back sixty-six years from the second year of Claudius' reign, the time of his birth falls in the thirteenth year of the reign of Severus. But he did not tell anyone the month in which he was born, nor his birthday, since he did not think it right to sacrifice or give a feast on his own birthday; and yet on the traditional birthdays of Plato and Socrates he sacrificed and gave his companions a feast, when those of the companions who were able also had to read out a discourse before those who had come together.
paragraphs.greek: ἀναψηφίζουσι δὲ ἡμῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ δευτέρου ἔτους τῆς Κλαυδίου βασιλείας εἰς τοὐπίσω ἔτη ἓξ τε καὶ ἑξήκοντα ὁ χρόνος αὐτῷ τῆς γενέσεως εἰς τὸ τρισκαιδέκατον ἔτος τῆς Σευήρου βασιλείας πίπτει. οὔτε δὲ τὸν μῆνα δεδήλωκέ τινι καθ’ ὃν γεγένηται, οὔτε τὴν γενέθλιον ἡμέραν, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ θύειν ἢ ἑστιᾶν τινα τοῖς αὐτοῦ γενεθλίοις ἠξίου, καίπερ ἐν τοῖς Πλάτωνος καὶ Σωκράτους παραδεδομένοις γενεθλίοις θύων τε καὶ ἑστιῶν τοὺς ἑταίρους, ὅτε καὶ λόγον ἔδει τῶν ἑταίρων τοὺς δυνατοὺς ἐπὶ τῶν συνελθόντων ἀναγνῶναι.
notes: The thirteenth year of the emperor Septimius Severus is AD 205, in the modern reckoning. The birthdays of Socrates and Plato were kept on the sixth and seventh of the Athenian month Thargelion (Plutarch, Table Talk VIII.1).

paragraphs.modern: These things, however, he often told us about himself in conversation. He kept going to his nurse, though he was already going to school to a teacher of letters, until he was eight years old, and baring her breasts was eager to suck; but once, hearing someone say that he was a wretched child, he was ashamed and stopped.
paragraphs.greek: ἃ μέντοι ἡμῖν αὐτὸς ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις πολλάκις διηγεῖτο, ἦν τοιαῦτα. προσφοιτᾶν μὲν γὰρ τῇ τροφῷ καίπερ εἰς γραμματοδιδασκάλου ἀπιόντα ἄχρις ὀγδόου ἔτους ἀπὸ γενέσεως ὄντα καὶ τοὺς μαζοὺς γυμνοῦντα θηλάζειν προθυμεῖσθαι· ἀκούσαντα δέ ποτε, ὅτι ἀτηρόν ἐστι παιδίον, ἀποσχέσθαι αἰδεσθέντα.

flags.taylor: he was told he was a " perverted imp,"
flags.why: The Greek ἀτηρὸν παιδίον is "a naughty (or wretched) child", a nurse's scolding; "perverted" is MacKenna's.

paragraphs.modern: In his twenty-eighth year he set out for philosophy, and was introduced to the teachers who had a name at Alexandria at that time; and he came away from their lectures downcast and full of sorrow, so that he told one of his friends what he was going through. The friend, understanding what his soul wanted, took him to Ammonius, whom he had not yet tried. He went in, heard him, and said to his companion: "This is the man I was looking for." And from that day he stayed with Ammonius continually, and gained such a mastery in philosophy that he was eager to get experience as well of the philosophy practised among the Persians and of the philosophy that flourishes among the Indians.
paragraphs.greek: εἰκοστὸν δὲ καὶ ὄγδοον ἔτος αὐτὸν ἄγοντα ὁρμῆσαι ἐπὶ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ τοῖς τότε κατὰ τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν εὐδοκιμοῦσι συσταθέντα κατιέναι ἐκ τῆς ἀκροάσεως αὐτῶν κατηφῆ καὶ λύπης πλήρη, ὡς καί τινι τῶν φίλων διηγεῖσθαι ἃ πάσχει· τὸν δὲ συνέντα αὐτοῦ τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ βούλημα ἀπενέγκαι πρὸς Ἀμμώνιον, οὗ μηδέπω πεπείρατο. τὸν δὲ εἰσελθόντα καὶ ἀκούσαντα φάναι πρὸς τὸν ἑταῖρον· τοῦτον ἐζήτουν. καὶ ἀπ’ ἐκείνης τῆς ἡμέρας συνεχῶς τῷ Ἀμμωνίῳ παραμένοντα τοσαύτην ἕξιν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ κτήσασθαι, ὡς καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς Πέρσαις ἐπιτηδευομένης πεῖραν λαβεῖν σπεῦσαι καὶ τῆς παρ’ Ἰνδοῖς κατορθουμένης.

flags.taylor: At twenty he was caught by the passion for philosophy
flags.why: The Greek says "in his twenty-eighth year" (εἰκοστὸν δὲ καὶ ὄγδοον ἔτος): MacKenna drops the eight. The count matters, since Porphyry then has him study eleven years with Ammonius and join Gordian's army at thirty-nine.

notes: Ammonius (called Saccas by later writers) left no writings; what he taught is known only through his pupils, of whom Plotinus is the greatest.

paragraphs.modern: When the emperor Gordian was about to march against the Persians, he gave himself to the army and went in with it, being already in his thirty-ninth year; for he had stayed studying with Ammonius for eleven whole years. When Gordian was killed in Mesopotamia, he escaped with difficulty and came through safely to Antioch. And when Philip had taken power, being forty years old, he went up to Rome.
paragraphs.greek: Γορδιανοῦ δὲ τοῦ βασιλέως ἐπὶ τοὺς Πέρσας παριέναι μέλλοντος δοὺς ἑαυτὸν τῷ στρατοπέδῳ συνεισῄει ἔτος ἤδη τριακοστὸν ἄγων καὶ ἔννατον. ἕνδεκα γὰρ ὅλων ἐτῶν παραμένων τῷ Ἀμμωνίῳ συνεσχόλασε. τοῦ δὲ Γορδιανοῦ περὶ τὴν Μεσοποταμίαν ἀναιρεθέντος μόλις φεύγων εἰς τὴν Ἀντιόχειαν διεσώθη. καὶ Φιλίππου τὴν βασιλείαν κρατήσαντος τεσσαράκοντα γεγονὼς ἔτη εἰς τὴν Ῥώμην ἄνεισιν.
notes: Gordian III marched against the Persians in 242 and died in Mesopotamia in 244; Philip the Arab followed him (modern dates).

paragraphs.modern: Erennius, Origen and Plotinus had made an agreement to reveal nothing of the teachings of Ammonius, which he had made clear to them in his lectures; and Plotinus kept to it: he met with some of those who came to him, but kept Ammonius' teachings undisclosed. Erennius was the first to break the agreement, and Origen followed Erennius, who had gone first. But Origen wrote nothing except the treatise On the daemons and, under Gallienus, That the king is the only maker. Plotinus went on for a long time writing nothing, but made his lectures from his time with Ammonius; and so he went on for ten whole years, meeting with some people but writing nothing. His lectures, since he urged those who were with him to ask questions themselves, were full of disorder and much idle talk, as Amelius told us.
paragraphs.greek: Ἐρεννίῳ δὲ καὶ Ὠριγένει καὶ Πλωτίνῳ συνθηκῶν γεγονυιῶν μηδὲν ἐκκαλύπτειν τῶν Ἀμμωνίου δογμάτων, ἃ δὴ ἐν ταῖς ἀκροάσεσιν αὐτοῖς ἀνεκεκάθαρτο, ἔμενε καὶ ὁ Πλωτῖνος συνὼν μέν τισι τῶν προσιόντων, τηρῶν δὲ ἀνέκπυστα τὰ παρὰ τοῦ Ἀμμωνίου δόγματα. Ἐρεννίου δὲ πρώτου τὰς συνθήκας παραβάντος Ὠριγένης μὲν ἠκολούθει τῷ φθάσαντι Ἐρεννίῳ. ἔγραψε δὲ οὐδὲν πλὴν τὸ περὶ τῶν δαιμόνων σύγγραμμα καὶ ἐπὶ Γαλιήνου, ὅτι μόνος ποιητὴς ὁ βασιλεύς. Πλωτῖνος δὲ ἄχρι μὲν πολλοῦ γράφων οὐδὲν διετέλεσεν, ἐκ δὲ τῆς Ἀμμωνίου συνουσίας ποιούμενος τὰς διατριβάς· καὶ οὕτως ὅλων ἐτῶν δέκα διετέλεσε, συνὼν μέν τισι, γράφων δὲ οὐδέν. ἦν δὲ ἡ διατριβή, ὡς ἂν αὐτοὺς ζητεῖν προτρεπομένου τοὺς συνόντας, ἀταξίας πλήρης καὶ πολλῆς φλυαρίας, ὡς Ἀμέλιος ἡμῖν διηγεῖτο.
notes: This Origen is the Platonist, Plotinus' fellow pupil under Ammonius; whether he is the same man as Origen the Christian writer, who also heard Ammonius, is a question modern scholars still argue.
ποιητής is both "maker" and "poet": the title can mean that the king of all is the only maker of the world.

paragraphs.modern: Amelius came to him when he was in his third year in Rome, in the third year of Philip's reign, and stayed until the first year of Claudius' reign, so that he was with him twenty-four whole years. When he came he already had a training from his time with Lysimachus, and in hard work he surpassed all those of his day, since he had copied and collected almost all the works of Numenius and learned most of them by heart. Making notes from the meetings, he put together about a hundred books of notes, which he has given to Ustillianus Hesychius of Apamea, whom he adopted as his son.
paragraphs.greek: προσῆλθε δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ Ἀμέλιος τρίτον ἔτος ἄγοντι ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ κατὰ τὸ τρίτον τῆς Φιλίππου βασιλείας ἔτος καὶ ἄχρι τοῦ πρώτου ἔτους τῆς Κλαυδίου βασιλείας παραμείνας ἔτη ὅλα συγγέγονεν εἴκοσι καὶ τέσσαρα, ἕξιν μὲν ἔχων ὅτε προσῆλθεν ἀπὸ τῆς Λυσιμάχου συνουσίας, φιλοπονίᾳ δὲ ὑπερβαλλόμενος τῶν καθ’ αὐτὸν πάντων διὰ τὸ καὶ σχεδὸν πάντα τὰ Νουμηνίου καὶ γράψαι καὶ συναγαγεῖν καὶ σχεδὸν τὰ πλεῖστα ἐκμαθεῖν· σχόλια δὲ ἐκ τῶν συνουσιῶν ποιούμενος ἑκατόν που βιβλία συνέταξε τῶν σχολίων, ἃ Οὐστιλλιανῷ Ἡσυχίῳ τῷ Ἀπαμεῖ, ὃν υἱὸν ἔθετο, κεχάρισται.

flags.taylor: presented to Hostilianus of Apamea
flags.why: The Greek names him Ustillianus Hesychius (Οὐστιλλιανῷ Ἡσυχίῳ) of Apamea; MacKenna gives one name, in another form.

notes: Numenius of Apamea was a Platonist of the second century, known now only from fragments; in chapter 17 Porphyry answers those who said that Plotinus took his ideas from him.

paragraphs.modern: In the tenth year of Gallienus' reign I, Porphyry, coming from Greece with Antonius of Rhodes, found Amelius in his eighteenth year with Plotinus, though he had not yet dared to write anything except his notes, which had not yet come to a hundred in number. In the tenth year of Gallienus' reign Plotinus was about fifty-nine years old. And I, Porphyry, was thirty years old myself when I first met him.
paragraphs.greek: τῷ δεκάτῳ δὲ ἔτει τῆς Γαλιήνου βασιλείας ἐγὼ Πορφύριος ἐκ τῆς Ἑλλάδος μετὰ Ἀντωνίου τοῦ Ῥοδίου γεγονὼς καταλαμβάνω μὲν τὸν Ἀμέλιον ὀκτωκαιδέκατον ἔτος ἔχοντα τῆς πρὸς Πλωτῖνον συνουσίας, μηδὲν δέ πω γράφειν τολμήσαντα πλὴν τῶν σχολίων, ἃ οὐδέπω εἰς ἑκατὸν τὸ πλῆθος αὐτῷ συνῆκτο. ἦν δὲ ὁ Πλωτῖνος τῷ δεκάτῳ ἔτει τῆς Γαλιήνου βασιλείας ἀμφὶ τὰ πεντήκοντα ἔτη καὶ ἐννέα. ἐγὼ δὲ Πορφύριος τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῷ συγγέγονα αὐτὸς ὢν τότε ἐτῶν τριάκοντα.
notes: The tenth year of Gallienus is AD 262-263, in the modern reckoning.

paragraphs.modern: From the first year of Gallienus' reign, however, Plotinus had been urged to write on the subjects that came up, and by the tenth year of Gallienus' reign, when I, Porphyry, first came to know him, he is found to have written twenty-one books, which I also got hold of, though they had been given out to few. For the giving out was not yet easy, nor done lightly, nor simply and readily, but with every care in judging those who received them.
paragraphs.greek: ἀπὸ μέντοι τοῦ πρώτου ἔτους τῆς Γαλιήνου ἀρχῆς προτραπεὶς ὁ Πλωτῖνος γράφειν τὰς ἐμπιπτούσας ὑποθέσεις [εἰς] τὸ δέκατον ἔτος τῆς Γαλιήνου ἀρχῆς, ὅτε τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῷ ἐγὼ ὁ Πορφύριος ἐγνωρίσθην, γράψας εὑρίσκεται εἴκοσι καὶ ἓν βιβλίον, ἃ καὶ κατείληφα ἐκδεδομένα ὀλίγοις. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἦν πω ῥᾳδία ἡ ἔκδοσις οὐδὲ εὐσυνειδήτως ἐγίγνετο οὐδ’ ἁπλῶς κἀκ τοῦ ῥᾴστου, ἀλλὰ μετὰ πάσης κρίσεως τῶν λαμβανόντων.

flags.taylor: the distribution was grudging and secret
flags.why: The Greek says only that the books were not given out easily or lightly, "but with every care in judging those who received them"; "secret" is MacKenna's.

paragraphs.modern:
These were the writings; and since he did not give them titles himself, each person gave each a title of his own. The titles that won out are these; and I shall set down the first words of the books as well, so that each of the books named can easily be recognised from its first words:
[1, I.6] On beauty. It begins: "Beauty is mostly in sight."
[2, IV.7] On the immortality of the soul. It begins: "Whether each of us is immortal."
[3, III.1] On destiny. It begins: "All the things that come to be."
[4, IV.2] On the being of the soul. It begins: "The being of the soul."
[5, V.9] On intellect, the forms, and what is. It begins: "All human beings, from the time they come to be."
[6, IV.8] On the descent of the soul into bodies. It begins: "Often, waking up."
[7, V.4] How what comes after the first comes from the first; and on the One. It begins: "If there is anything after the first."
[8, IV.9] Whether all souls are one. It begins: "Is it so, that just as the soul."
[9, VI.9] On the Good, or the One. It begins: "All the things that are."
[10, V.1] On the three first realities. It begins: "What is it, then, that has made the souls."
[11, V.2] On the coming to be and the order of what comes after the first. It begins: "The One is all things."
[12, II.4] On the two kinds of matter. It begins: "What is called matter."
[13, III.9] Various considerations. It begins: "Intellect, he says, sees the forms that are in."
[14, II.2] On the circular movement. It begins: "Why does it move in a circle."
[15, III.4] On the daemon allotted to us. It begins: "Of some, the realities."
[16, I.9] On going out of life reasonably. It begins: "You shall not lead it out, lest it go out."
[17, II.6] On quality. It begins: "Are being and substance."
[18, V.7] Whether there are forms of individuals too. It begins: "Whether there is a form of the individual too."
[19, I.2] On the virtues. It begins: "Since evils are here."
[20, I.3] On dialectic. It begins: "What art, or method."
[21, IV.1] How the soul is said to be between the undivided and the divided being. It begins: "In the intelligible world."
paragraphs.greek: ἦν δὲ καὶ τὰ γεγραμμένα ταῦτα, ἃ διὰ τὸ μὴ αὐτὸν ἐπιγράφειν ἄλλος ἄλλο ἑκάστῳ τοὐπίγραμμα ἐτίθει. αἱ δ’ οὖν κρατήσασαι ἐπιγραφαί εἰσιν αἵδε· θήσω δὲ καὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν βιβλίων, εἰς τὸ εὐεπίγνωστον εἶναι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἕκαστον τῶν δηλουμένων βιβλίων· περὶ τοῦ καλοῦ. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ καλόν ἐστι μὲν ἐν ὄψει πλεῖστον. περὶ ψυχῆς ἀθανασίας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· εἰ δέ ἐστιν ἀθάνατος ἕκαστος. περὶ εἱμαρμένης. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· πάντα τὰ γινόμενα. περὶ οὐσίας τῆς ψυχῆς. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσίαν. περὶ νοῦ καὶ τῶν ἰδεῶν καὶ τοῦ ὄντος. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· πάντες ἄνθρωποι ἐξ ἀρχῆς γενόμενοι. περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ σώματα καθόδου τῆς ψυχῆς. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· πολλάκις ἐγειρόμενος. πῶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου τὸ μετὰ τὸ πρῶτον· καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἑνός. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· εἴ τι ἐστὶ μετὰ τὸ πρῶτον. εἰ πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ μία. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρα ὥσπερ ψυχήν. περὶ τἀγαθοῦ ἢ τοῦ ἑνός. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἅπαντα τὰ ὄντα. περὶ τῶν τριῶν ἀρχικῶν ὑποστάσεων. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τί ποτε ἄρα ἐστὶ τὸ πεποιηκὸς τὰς ψυχάς. περὶ γενέσεως καὶ τάξεως τῶν μετὰ τὸ πρῶτον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ ἓν πάντα. περὶ τῶν δύο ὑλῶν. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὴν λεγομένην ὕλην. ἐπισκέψεις διάφοροι. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· νοῦς, φησιν, ὁρᾷ ἐνούσας ἰδέας. περὶ τῆς κυκλοφορίας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· διὰ τί κύκλῳ κινεῖται. περὶ τοῦ εἰληχότος ἡμᾶς δαίμονος. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τῶν μὲν αἱ ὑποστάσεις. περὶ εὐλόγου ἐξαγωγῆς. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· οὐκ ἐξάξεις, ἵνα μὴ ἐξίῃ. περὶ ποιότητος. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρα τὸ ὂν καὶ ἡ οὐσία. εἰ καὶ τῶν καθέκαστα εἰσὶν ἰδέαι. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· εἰ καὶ τῶν καθέκαστον. περὶ ἀρετῶν. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐπειδὴ τὰ κακὰ ἐνταῦθα. περὶ διαλεκτικῆς. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τίς τέχνη ἢ μέθοδος. πῶς ἡ ψυχὴ τῆς ἀμερίστου καὶ μεριστῆς οὐσίας μέση εἶναι λέγεται. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τῷ νοητῷ.

flags.taylor: On our Tutelary Spirit (II. 2)
flags.why: The fifteenth book, "On the daemon allotted to us", is III.4 in the Enneads, not II.2, which is the fourteenth, "On the circular movement". The Ennead places are MacKenna's additions.

notes: The numbers and Ennead places in square brackets are the Workshop's, not Porphyry's: the place of each book in his count by date of writing, and where he set it in his edition (the Workshop numbers the Enneads as First1KGreek's text does, in which IV.1 is the short treatise that begins "In the intelligible world"). MacKenna leaves out the first words, and adds his own Ennead places; he gives IV.1 for both the fourth book and the twenty-first.

The title of the fifteenth book recalls Plato's Phaedo (107d): the daemon "allotted" to each in life leads the soul after death. The sixteenth echoes the Phaedo too (61c-62c): we must not take ourselves out of life.

paragraphs.modern: These, then, twenty-one in all, are found to have been written when I, Porphyry, first came to him; Plotinus was then in his fifty-ninth year.
paragraphs.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν εἴκοσι καὶ ἓν ὄντα, ὅτε αὐτῷ τὸ πρῶτον προσῆλθον ὁ Πορφύριος, εὕρηται γεγραμμένα· πεντηκοστὸν δὲ καὶ ἔννατον ἔτος ἦγε τότε ὁ Πλωτῖνος.

paragraphs.modern: I was with him this year and five years after it (for I, Porphyry, had come to Rome a little before the tenth year, while Plotinus was keeping the summer months free of lectures, though meeting people otherwise in conversation). In these six years, as many questions were examined in the meetings, and Amelius and I asked him to write, he wrote two books, [22-23, VI.4-5] That being, one and the same, is everywhere whole. The first of these has the beginning: "Is it the soul that is everywhere"; the second's beginning is: "The one and the same everywhere." Next he wrote two more: one [24, V.6], That what is beyond being does not think, and what is the first thinker and what the second, which begins: "One thing thinks something other"; the other [25, II.5], On the potential and the actual, which begins: "Something is said to be potential."
paragraphs.greek: συγγεγονὼς δὲ αὐτῷ τοῦτό τε τὸ ἔτος καὶ ἐφεξῆς ἄλλα ἔτη πέντε — ὀλίγον γάρ τι πρότερον τῆς δεκαετίας ἐγεγόνειν ὁ Πορφύριος ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ, τοῦ Πλωτίνου τὰς θερινὰς μὲν ἄγοντος ἀργούς, συνόντος δὲ ἄλλως ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις — ἐν δὴ τοῖς ἓξ ἔτεσι τούτοις πολλῶν ἐξετάσεων ἐν ταῖς συνουσίαις γιγνομένων καὶ γράφειν αὐτὸν ἀξιούντων Ἀμελίου τε καὶ ἐμοῦ, γράφει μὲν περὶ τοῦ τὸ ὂν πανταχοῦ ὅλον εἶναι ἓν καὶ ταὐτὸν βιβλία δύο. τούτων δὲ τὸ πρῶτον ἀρχὴν ἔχει· ἆρά γε ἡ ψυχὴ πανταχοῦ· τοῦ δὲ δευτέρου ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ ἓν καὶ ταὐτὸν πανταχοῦ. γράφει δὲ ἐφεξῆς ἄλλα δύο, ὧν τὸ μὲν περὶ τοῦ τὸ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ ὄντος μὴ νοεῖν καὶ τί τὸ πρώτως νοοῦν καὶ τί τὸ δευτέρως, οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ μέν ἐστι νοοῦν ἄλλο· τὸ δὲ περὶ τοῦ δυνάμει καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ, οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· λέγεται τὸ μὲν δυνάμει.

flags.taylor: Unity (II. 4, 5)
flags.why: The two books "That being, one and the same, is everywhere whole" are VI.4 and VI.5 of the Enneads, not II.4 and II.5 (which are "On matter" and "On the potential and the actual").

paragraphs.modern:
[26, III.6] On the impassibility of the bodiless. It begins: "Saying that perceptions are not affections."
[27, IV.3] On the soul, first. It begins: "About the soul, all the questions we must raise."
[28, IV.4] On the soul, second. It begins: "What, then, will it say."
[29, IV.5] On the soul, third; or, How we see. It begins: "Since we put off."
[30, III.8] On contemplation. It begins: "Playing, then, at first."
[31, V.8] On intelligible beauty. It begins: "Since we say."
[32, V.5] That the intelligibles are not outside intellect, and on the Good. It begins: "Intellect, the true intellect."
[33, II.9] Against the Gnostics. It begins: "Since, then, it has appeared to us."
[34, VI.6] On numbers. It begins: "Is multiplicity."
[35, II.8] How things seen far off look small. It begins: "Is it that things seen far off."
[36, I.5] Whether being happy lies in length of time. It begins: "Being happy."
[37, II.7] On complete blending. It begins: "About what is called."
[38, VI.7] How the many forms came to be, and on the Good. It begins: "Sending into coming to be, the god."
[39, VI.8] On what is willed. It begins: "Is it, even in the case of the gods."
[40, II.1] On the cosmos. It begins: "Saying that the cosmos always."
[41, IV.6] On perception and memory. It begins: "Saying that perceptions are not imprints."
[42, VI.1] On the kinds of being, first. It begins: "About the things that are, how many and which."
[43, VI.2] On the kinds of being, second. It begins: "Since, about the so-called."
[44, VI.3] On the kinds of being, third. It begins: "About substance, how it seems."
[45, III.7] On eternity and time. It begins: "Eternity and time."
paragraphs.greek: περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀσωμάτων ἀπαθείας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὰς αἰσθήσεις οὐ πάθη λέγοντες. περὶ ψυχῆς πρῶτον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· περὶ ψυχῆς ὅσα ἀπορήσαντας δεῖ. περὶ ψυχῆς δεύτερον· οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τί οὖν ἐρεῖ. περὶ ψυχῆς τρίτον ἢ περὶ τοῦ πῶς ὁρῶμεν. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐπειδήπερ ὑπερεθέμεθα. περὶ θεωρίας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· παίζοντες δὴ τὴν πρώτην. περὶ τοῦ νοητοῦ κάλλους. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐπειδή φαμεν. ὅτι οὐκ ἔξω τοῦ νοῦ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ περὶ νοῦ καὶ τἀγαθοῦ. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸν νοῦν τὸν ἀληθῆ νοῦν. πρὸς τοὺς γνωστικούς. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν ἐφάνη ἡμῖν. περὶ ἀριθμῶν. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρά ἐστι τὸ πλῆθος. πῶς τὰ πόρρω ὁρώμενα μικρὰ φαίνεται. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρά γε τὰ πόρρω ὁρώμενα. εἰ ἐν παρατάσει χρόνου τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ εὐδαιμονεῖν. περὶ τῆς δι’ ὅλων κράσεως. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· περὶ τῆς δι’ ὅλων λεγομένης. πῶς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἰδεῶν ὑπέστη καὶ περὶ τἀγαθοῦ. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· εἰς γένεσιν πέμπων ὁ θεός. περὶ τοῦ ἑκουσίου. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρ’ ἐστι περὶ θεῶν. περὶ τοῦ κόσμου. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸν κόσμον ἀεὶ λέγοντες. περὶ αἰσθήσεως καὶ μνήμης. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὰς αἰσθήσεις οὐ τυπώσεις. περὶ τῶν τοῦ ὄντος γενῶν πρῶτον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· περὶ τῶν ὄντων πόσα καὶ τίνα. περὶ τῶν τοῦ ὄντος γενῶν δεύτερον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἐπειδὴ περὶ τῶν λεγομένων. περὶ τῶν τοῦ ὄντος γενῶν τρίτον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· περὶ μὲν τῆς οὐσίας ὅπῃ δοκεῖ. περὶ αἰῶνος καὶ χρόνου. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ τὸν χρόνον.

flags.taylor: After these come the following twenty
flags.why: Porphyry simply goes on with the list; the heading, and the count of twenty, are MacKenna's.

flags.taylor: On the Impassibility of the Bodiless (III. 5)
flags.why: This book is III.6 of the Enneads; III.5 is "On love", the fiftieth.

paragraphs.modern: These twenty-four, which he wrote in the six-year period of my, Porphyry's, presence, taking their subjects from problems that came up at the time, as we have shown from the headings of each of the books, together with the twenty-one from before our stay, make forty-five in all.
paragraphs.greek: ταῦτα τὰ εἴκοσι καὶ τέτταρα ὄντα, ὅσα ἐν τῷ ἑξαέτει χρόνῳ τῆς παρουσίας ἐμοῦ Πορφυρίου ἔγραψεν, ἐκ προσκαίρων προβλημάτων τὰς ὑποθέσεις λαβόντα, ὡς ἐκ τῶν κεφαλαίων ἑκάστου τῶν βιβλίων ἐδηλώσαμεν, μετὰ τῶν πρὸ τῆς ἐπιδημίας ἡμῶν εἴκοσι καὶ ἑνὸς τὰ πάντα γίνεται τεσσαράκοντα πέντε.

paragraphs.modern:
While I was living in Sicily (for I had withdrawn there about the fifteenth year of Gallienus' reign), Plotinus wrote five books and sent them to me:
[46, I.4] On happiness. It begins: "Living well and being happy."
[47, III.2] On providence, first. It begins: "To chance."
[48, III.3] On providence, second. It begins: "What, then, do we think about these things."
[49, V.3] On the knowing realities and what is beyond. It begins: "Must what thinks itself be manifold."
[50, III.5] On love. It begins: "About love, whether it is a god."
paragraphs.greek: ἐν δὲ τῇ Σικελίᾳ διατρίβοντός μου· ἐκεῖ γὰρ ἀνεχώρησα περὶ τὸ πεντεκαιδέκατον ἔτος τῆς βασιλείας Γαλιήνου· ὁ Πλωτῖνος γράψας πέντε βιβλία ἀπέστειλέ μοι ταῦτα· περὶ εὐδαιμονίας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ εὖ ζῆν καὶ εὐδαιμονεῖν. περὶ προνοίας πρῶτον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τὸ μὲν αὐτομάτῳ. περὶ προνοίας δεύτερον. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· τί τοίνυν δοκεῖ περὶ τούτων. περὶ τῶν γνωριστικῶν ὑποστάσεων καὶ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρα τὸ νοοῦν ἑαυτὸ ποικίλον δεῖ εἶναι. περὶ ἔρωτος. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· περὶ ἔρωτος πότερον θεός.

paragraphs.modern:
These, then, he sent in the first year of Claudius' reign; at the beginning of the second, when he died soon after, he sent these:
[51, I.8] What evils are. It begins: "Those who ask where evils come from."
[52, II.3] Whether the stars act. It begins: "The movement of the stars."
[53, I.1] What is the living being, and what is the human being. It begins: "Pleasures and pains."
[54, I.7] On the first good, or on happiness. It begins: "Could anyone say that another."
paragraphs.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν τῷ πρώτῳ ἔτει τῆς Κλαυδίου πέμπει βασιλείας· ἀρχομένου δὲ τοῦ δευτέρου, ὅτε καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον θνήσκει, πέμπει ταῦτα· τίνα τὰ κακά. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· οἱ ζητοῦντες πόθεν τὰ κακά. εἰ ποιεῖ τὰ ἄστρα. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἡ τῶν ἄστρων φορά. τί τὸ ζῷον καὶ τίς ὁ ἄνθρωπος. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἡδοναὶ καὶ λῦπαι. περὶ τοῦ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ ἢ περὶ εὐδαιμονίας. οὗ ἡ ἀρχή· ἆρα ἄν τις ἕτερον εἴποι.

flags.taylor: On the First Good ; or, On Happiness (I. 8)
flags.why: The last book, "On the first good", is I.7 of the Enneads; I.8 is "What evils are", the fifty-first.

paragraphs.modern: These, with the forty-five of the first and second writing, make fifty-four. And as they were written, some in his earlier age, some in his prime, and some when his body was worn out by illness, so the books have their strength. The first twenty-one are of slighter power, not yet having enough greatness for full vigour; those that came out in the middle period show his power at its height, and the twenty-four, except for the short ones, are the most complete; but the last nine were written when his power was already failing, and the last four more so than the five before them.
paragraphs.greek: ταῦτα μετὰ τῶν τετταράκοντα πέντε τῶν πρώτων καὶ δευτέρων γραφέντων γίνεται τέτταρα καὶ πεντήκοντα. ὥσπερ δὲ ἐγράφη, τὰ μὲν κατὰ πρώτην ἡλικίαν, τὰ δὲ ἀκμάζοντος, τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ σώματος καταπονουμένου, οὕτω καὶ τῆς δυνάμεως ἔχει τὰ βιβλία. τὰ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτα εἴκοσι καὶ ἓν ἐλαφροτέρας ἐστὶ δυνάμεως καὶ οὐδέπω πρὸς εὐτονίαν ἀρκοῦν μέγεθος ἐχούσης, τὰ δὲ τῆς μέσης ἐκδόσεως τυχόντα τὸ ἀκμαῖον τῆς δυνάμεως ἐμφαίνει καὶ ἔστι τὰ εἰκοσιτέσσαρα πλὴν τῶν βραχέων τελεώτατα, τὰ μέντοι τελευταῖα ἐννέα ὑφειμένης ἤδη τῆς δυνάμεως γέγραπται καὶ μᾶλλόν γε τὰ τελευταῖα τέσσαρα ἢ τὰ πρὸ τούτων πέντε.

flags.taylor: early manhood, vigorous prime, worn-out constitution
flags.why: The Greek κατὰ πρώτην ἡλικίαν is "in his earlier age": by Porphyry's own count Plotinus was about forty-eight to fifty-nine when he wrote the first twenty-one, not in "early manhood".

notes: Modern readers have doubted this judgement, which ranks the books by Porphyry's own years with Plotinus: the first twenty-one include On beauty (I.6) and On the Good, or the One (VI.9).

paragraphs.modern: He had many hearers, and as followers who were with him for the sake of philosophy, Amelius from Etruria, whose proper name was Gentilianus, though he himself wanted to be called Amerius, with an r, saying that it suited him to be named from amereia, being without parts, rather than from ameleia, carelessness. He had also a doctor, Paulinus of Scythopolis, whom Amelius used to call Mikkalos, "little one", a man full of things he had misheard. And he had as a companion a doctor from Alexandria, Eustochius, who came to know him towards the end of his life and stayed, caring for him, until his death; giving his time to Plotinus' teachings alone, he took on the character of a true philosopher.
paragraphs.greek: ἔσχε δὲ ἀκροατὰς μὲν πλείους, ζηλωτὰς δὲ καὶ διὰ φιλοσοφίαν συνόντας Ἀμέλιόν τε ἀπὸ τῆς Τουσκίας, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα ἦν Γεντιλιανὸς τὸ κύριον, αὐτὸς δὲ διὰ τοῦ ρ Ἀμέριον αὐτὸν καλεῖν ἠξίου ἀπὸ τῆς ἀμερείας ἢ τῆς ἀμελείας πρέπειν αὐτῷ καλεῖσθαι λέγων. ἔσχε δὲ καὶ ἰατρικόν τινα Σκυθοπολίτην Παυλῖνον, ὃν ὁ Ἀμέλιος Μίκκαλον προσηγόρευε, παρακουσμάτων πλήρη γεγονότα. ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ Ἀλεξανδρέα Εὐστόχιον ἰατρικὸν ἔσχεν ἑταῖρον, ὃς περὶ τὰ τελευταῖα τῆς ἡλικίας γνωρισθεὶς αὐτῷ διέμενε θεραπεύων ἄχρι τοῦ θανάτου καὶ μόνοις τοῖς Πλωτίνου σχολάζων ἕξιν περιεβάλλετο γνησίου φιλοσόφου.

flags.taylor: from Amereia, Unification,
flags.why: ἀμέρεια is "being without parts", indivisibility, which the intelligible has; MacKenna's "Unification" is near the sense, but not the word.

paragraphs.modern: Zoticus, too, was with him, a critic and a poet, who made corrected editions of Antimachus and turned the story of Atlantis into a poem, very poetically; his sight failed him, and he died a little before Plotinus' death. Paulinus also died before Plotinus. He had also a companion Zethus, an Arab by birth, who married the daughter of Theodosius, a companion of Ammonius. He too was a doctor, and Plotinus loved him dearly; and since he was a man of civic affairs, with leanings towards civic life, Plotinus tried to hold him back from it. He treated him as one of his own, so that he would even withdraw to his country place six miles from Minturnae, the fields that Castricius, called Firmus, had owned. Castricius was of all the men of our time the greatest lover of beautiful things; he revered Plotinus, served Amelius in everything like a good servant, and was devoted to me, Porphyry, in everything as to a true brother. He too, then, revered Plotinus, though he had chosen the civic life.
paragraphs.greek: συνῆν δὲ καὶ Ζωτικὸς κριτικός τε καὶ ποιητικός, ὃς καὶ τὰ Ἀντιμάχου διορθωτικὰ πεποίηται καὶ τὸν Ἀτλαντικὸν εἰς ποίησιν μετέβαλε πάνυ ποιητικῶς, συγχυθεὶς δὲ τὰς ὄψεις πρὸ ὀλίγου τῆς Πλωτίνου τελευτῆς ἀπέθανεν. ἔφθασε δὲ καὶ ὁ Παυλῖνος προαποθανὼν τοῦ Πλωτίνου. ἔσχε δὲ καὶ Ζῆθον ἑταῖρον, Ἀράβιον τὸ γένος, Θεοδοσίου τοῦ Ἀμμωνίου γενομένου ἑταίρου εἰς γάμον λαβόντα θυγατέρα. ἦν δὲ καὶ οὗτος ἰατρικὸς καὶ σφόδρα πεφίλητο τῷ Πλωτίνῳ· πολιτικὸν δὲ ὄντα καὶ ῥοπὰς ἔχοντα πολιτικὰς ἀναστέλλειν ὁ Πλωτῖνος ἐπειρᾶτο. ἐχρῆτο δὲ αὐτῷ οἰκείως, ὡς καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἀγροὺς πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀναχωρεῖν πρὸ ἓξ σημείων Μιντουρνῶν ὑπάρχοντας, οὓς Καστρίκιος ἐκέκτητο ὁ Φίρμος καλούμενος, ἀνδρῶν τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς φιλοκαλώτατος γεγονὼς καὶ τόν τε Πλωτῖνον σεβόμενος καὶ Ἀμελίῳ οἷα οἰκέτης ἀγαθὸς ἐν πᾶσιν ὑπηρετούμενος καὶ Πορφυρίῳ ἐμοὶ οἷα γνησίῳ ἀδελφῷ ἐν πᾶσι προσεσχηκώς. καὶ οὗτος οὖν ἐσέβετο Πλωτῖνον τὸν πολιτικὸν ᾑρημένος βίον.

flags.taylor: the political career in which he stood high
flags.why: The Greek says only that Zethus was a man of politics, "with political leanings" (ῥοπὰς ἔχοντα πολιτικάς), which Plotinus tried to check; that he "stood high" in it is MacKenna's.

notes: Antimachus of Colophon was an epic poet of about 400 BC; the story of Atlantis is told by Plato in the Timaeus (20d-25d) and Critias.

paragraphs.modern: Not a few members of the Senate also attended his lectures, of whom Marcellus Orrontius and Sabinillus worked hardest at philosophy. There was also Rogatianus, of the Senate, who had gone so far in turning away from this life that he gave up all his property, sent away all his servants, and gave up his rank as well; when he was about to go out as praetor, with the attendants waiting, he would neither go out nor take any care of the office. He would not even choose a house of his own to live in, but went round to some of his friends and acquaintances, dining and sleeping there, and eating only every other day. And from this renunciation, and this carelessness about the needs of life, though he had had gout so badly that he was carried in a chair, he recovered his strength; and though he had not been able to stretch out his hands, he came to use them much more easily than those who live by the crafts of their hands. Plotinus welcomed him, and kept praising him above all, holding him up as a good pattern to those who do philosophy.
paragraphs.greek: ἠκροῶντο δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς συγκλήτου οὐκ ὀλίγοι, ὧν ἔργον ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ μάλιστα ἐποίουν Μάρκελλος Ὀρρόντιος καὶ Σαβινίλλος. ἦν δὲ καὶ Ῥογατιανὸς ἐκ τῆς συγκλήτου, ὃς εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀποστροφῆς τοῦ βίου τούτου προκεχωρήκει, ὡς πάσης μὲν κτήσεως ἀποστῆναι, πάντα δὲ οἰκέτην ἀποπέμψασθαι, ἀποστῆναι δὲ καὶ τοῦ ἀξιώματος, καὶ πραίτωρα προϊέναι μέλλοντα παρόντων τῶν ὑπηρετῶν μήτε προελθεῖν μήτε φροντίσαι τῆς λειτουργίας, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ οἰκίαν ἑαυτοῦ ἑλέσθαι κατοικεῖν, ἀλλὰ πρός τινας τῶν φίλων καὶ συνήθων φοιτῶντα ἐκεῖ τε δειπνεῖν κἀκεῖ καθεύδειν, σιτεῖσθαι δὲ παρὰ μίαν· ἀφ’ ἧς δὴ ἀποστάσεως καὶ ἀφροντιστίας τοῦ βίου ποδαγρῶντα μὲν οὕτως, ὡς καὶ δίφρῳ βαστάζεσθαι, ἀναρρωσθῆναι, τὰς χεῖρας δὲ ἐκτεῖναι μὴ οἷόν τε ὄντα χρῆσθαι ταύταις πολὺ μᾶλλον εὐμαρῶς ἢ οἱ τὰς τέχνας διὰ τῶν χειρῶν μετιόντες. τοῦτον ἀπεδέχετο ὁ Πλωτῖνος καὶ ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα ἐπαινῶν διετέλει εἰς ἀγαθὸν παράδειγμα τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσι προβαλλόμενος.

flags.taylor: only one meal a day
flags.why: The Greek σιτεῖσθαι παρὰ μίαν is "to eat every other day", skipping a day between meals; MacKenna's "one meal a day" is a milder fast.

paragraphs.modern: There was also Serapion of Alexandria, at first a rhetorician, and later given to philosophical discussions as well, but he could not give up his weakness for money and money-lending. He had me too, Porphyry of Tyre, among his closest companions, and he asked me to correct his writings.
paragraphs.greek: συνῆν δὲ καὶ Σεραπίων Ἀλεξανδρεὺς ῥητορικὸς μὲν τὰ πρῶτα, μετὰ ταῦτα δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ φιλοσόφοις συνὼν λόγοις, τοῦ δὲ περὶ χρήματα καὶ τὸ δανείζειν μὴ δυνηθεὶς ἀποστῆναι ἐλαττώματος. ἔσχε δὲ καὶ ἐμὲ Πορφύριον Τύριον ὄντα ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα ἑταῖρον, ὃν καὶ διορθοῦν αὐτοῦ τὰ συγγράμματα ἠξίου.

paragraphs.modern: For once he had written something, he could never bear to take it up a second time, nor even to read it through once, because his sight did not serve him for reading. He wrote without forming the letters beautifully, without dividing the syllables clearly, and without caring for spelling: he held only to the sense [and the matter]; and he kept on doing the thing we all marvelled at to the end.
paragraphs.greek: γράψας γὰρ ἐκεῖνος δὶς τὸ γραφὲν μεταλαβεῖν οὐδέποτ’ ἂν ἠνέσχετο, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἅπαξ γοῦν ἀναγνῶναι καὶ διελθεῖν διὰ τὸ τὴν ὅρασιν μὴ ὑπηρετεῖσθαι αὐτῷ πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγνωσιν. ἔγραφε δὲ οὔτε εἰς κάλλος ἀποτυπούμενος τὰ γράμματα οὔτε εὐσήμως τὰς συλλαβὰς διαιρῶν οὔτε τῆς ὀρθογραφίας φροντίζων, ἀλλὰ μόνον τοῦ νοῦ [καὶ τῶν πραγμάτων] ἐχόμενος, καί, ὃ πάντες ἐθαυμάζομεν, ἐκεῖνο ποιῶν ἄχρι τελευτῆς διετέλεσε.

flags.taylor: in these habits, to our general surprise, he remained unchanged to the very end
flags.why: What "we all marvelled at" (ὃ πάντες ἐθαυμάζομεν) is what follows, "for he would complete the argument in himself...": his writing straight from a finished thought, not his careless habits.

paragraphs.modern: For he would complete the inquiry within himself from beginning to end, and then, putting what he had thought into writing, he would write out what he had set in order in his soul so continuously that he seemed to be copying from a book. Even when he was talking with someone and keeping the conversation going, he was at his own inquiry, so that he could meet what the conversation needed and at the same time keep his thought on what he was examining unbroken. When the person he was talking with had gone, he did not go over what he had written, because, as we have said, his sight was not enough for rereading; he would join on what came next, as if he had left no time between, while he was in conversation.
paragraphs.greek: συντελέσας γὰρ παρ’ ἑαυτῷ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἄχρι τέλους τὸ σκέμμα, ἔπειτα εἰς γραφὴν παραδιδοὺς ἃ ἔσκεπτο, συνεῖρεν οὕτως γράφων ἃ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ διέθηκεν, ὡς ἀπὸ βιβλίου δοκεῖν μεταλαβεῖν τὰ γραφόμενα· ἐπεὶ καὶ διαλεγόμενος πρός τινα καὶ συνείρων τὰς ὁμιλίας πρὸς τῷ σκέμματι ἦν, ὡς ἅμα τε ἀποπληροῦν τὸ ἀναγκαῖον τῆς ὁμιλίας καὶ τῶν ἐν σκέψει προκειμένων ἀδιάκοπον τηρεῖν τὴν διάνοιαν· ἀποστάντος γοῦν τοῦ προσδιαλεγομένου οὐδ’ ἐπαναλαβὼν τὰ γεγραμμένα, διὰ τὸ μὴ ἐπαρκεῖν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἀνάληψιν, ὡς εἰρήκαμεν, τὴν ὅρασιν, τὰ ἑξῆς ἂν ἐπισυνῆψεν, ὡς μηδένα διαστήσας χρόνον μεταξὺ ὅτε τὴν ὁμιλίαν ἐποιεῖτο.

flags.taylor: by someone entering on business
flags.why: The Greek says only "even when talking with someone and keeping the conversation going"; the visitor "entering on business" is MacKenna's.

paragraphs.modern: So he was present at once to himself and to others, and he would never relax his attention to himself, except in sleep; and sleep was kept away by the smallness of his food (often he would not even touch bread) and by his continual turning towards intellect.
paragraphs.greek: συνῆν οὖν καὶ ἑαυτῷ ἅμα καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, καὶ τήν γε πρὸς ἑαυτὸν προσοχὴν οὐκ ἄν ποτε ἐχάλασεν, ἢ μόνον ἐν τοῖς ὕπνοις, ὃν ἂν ἀπέκρουεν ἥ τε τῆς τροφῆς ὀλιγότης, οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄρτου πολλάκις ἂν ἥψατο, καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὸν νοῦν αὐτοῦ διαρκὴς ἐπιστροφή.

paragraphs.modern: He also had women who were greatly devoted to him: Gemina, in whose house he lived, and her daughter, also Gemina, named like her mother, and Amphiclea, who had become the wife of Ariston, the son of Iamblichus; they were greatly devoted to philosophy.
paragraphs.greek: ἔσχε δὲ καὶ γυναῖκας σφόδρα προσκειμένας, Γεμίναν τε, ἧς καὶ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ κατῴκει, καὶ τὴν ταύτης θυγατέρα Γεμίναν, ὁμοίως τῇ μητρὶ καλουμένην, Ἀμφίκλειάν τε τὴν Ἀρίστωνος τοῦ Ἰαμβλίχου υἱοῦ γεγονυῖαν γυναῖκα, σφόδρα φιλοσοφίᾳ προσκειμένας.
notes: This Iamblichus is not the philosopher, who was younger; who he was is not known.

paragraphs.modern: Many men and women of the noblest families, when they were about to die, brought him their children, boys and girls alike, and entrusted them to him with the rest of their property, as to a holy and divine guardian. So his house was full of boys and girls. Among them was Polemon, whose education he cared for, and he would often listen to him even when he was composing verses. He also put up with going over the accounts brought to him by those in charge of the children's affairs, and saw to it that they were exact, saying that, until the children took up philosophy, they must keep their possessions and incomes untouched and safe. And yet, though he provided for so many people the cares and attentions of life, he never relaxed, while he was awake, his tension towards intellect.
paragraphs.greek: πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄνδρες καὶ γυναῖκες ἀποθνήσκειν μέλλοντες τῶν εὐγενεστάτων φέροντες τὰ ἑαυτῶν τέκνα, ἄρρενάς τε ὁμοῦ καὶ θηλείας, ἐκείνῳ παρεδίδοσαν μετὰ τῆς ἄλλης οὐσίας ὡς ἱερῷ τινι καὶ θείῳ φύλακι. διὸ καὶ ἐπεπλήρωτο αὐτῷ ἡ οἰκία παίδων καὶ παρθένων. ἐν τούτοις δὲ ἦν καὶ Πολέμων, οὗ τῆς παιδεύσεως φροντίζων πολλάκις ἂν καὶ μέτρα ποιοῦντος ἠκροάσατο. ἠνείχετο δὲ καὶ τοὺς λογισμοὺς ἀναφερόντων τῶν ἐκείνοις παραμενόντων καὶ τῆς ἀκριβείας ἐπεμελεῖτο λέγων, ἕως ἂν μὴ φιλοσοφῶσιν, ἔχειν αὐτοὺς δεῖν τὰς κτήσεις καὶ τὰς προσόδους ἀνεπάφους τε καὶ σωζομένας. καὶ ὅμως τοσούτοις ἐπαρκῶν τὰς εἰς τὸν βίον φροντίδας τε καὶ ἐπιμελείας τὴν πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τάσιν οὐδέποτ’ ἂν ἐγρηγορὼς ἐχάλασεν.

flags.taylor: his intention towards the Supreme
flags.why: The Greek is τὴν πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τάσιν, his "tension towards intellect"; MacKenna's "the Supreme" sets it higher, at the One.

paragraphs.modern: He was gentle, too, and available to all who had any acquaintance at all with him. So, though he spent twenty-six whole years in Rome and settled many people's disputes with one another, he never made an enemy of any of the men in civic life.
paragraphs.greek: ἦν δὲ καὶ πρᾷος καὶ πᾶσιν ἐκκείμενος τοῖς ὁπωσοῦν πρὸς αὐτὸν συνήθειαν ἐσχηκόσι. διὸ εἴκοσι καὶ ἓξ ἐτῶν ὅλων ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ διατρίψας καὶ πλείστοις διαιτήσας τὰς πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀμφισβητήσεις οὐδένα τῶν πολιτικῶν ἐχθρόν ποτε ἔσχε.
notes: Twenty-six years: from 244, when he came to Rome at forty, to 270 (modern dates).

paragraphs.modern: Among those who claimed to do philosophy, Olympius of Alexandria, who had been for a short time a pupil of Ammonius, behaved with contempt towards him from love of being first; and he went so far in attacking him that he even tried to bring a star-stroke on him by magic. But when he found the attempt turning back on himself, he said to his friends that the power of Plotinus' soul was great, so great that it could throw back the attacks made on it onto those trying to harm him. Plotinus, though, felt Olympius' attempt, and said that at that moment his body was being pulled tight like a drawstring purse, his limbs being squeezed against one another. And Olympius, after often being in danger of suffering something himself rather than doing anything to Plotinus, stopped.
paragraphs.greek: τῶν δὲ φιλοσοφεῖν προσποιουμένων Ὀλύμπιος Ἀλεξανδρεύς, Ἀμμωνίου ἐπ’ ὀλίγον μαθητὴς γενόμενος, καταφρονητικῶς πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔσχε διὰ φιλοπρωτίαν· ὃς καὶ οὕτως αὐτῷ ἐπέθετο, ὥστε καὶ ἀστροβολῆσαι αὐτὸν μαγεύσας ἐπεχείρησεν. ἐπεὶ δὲ εἰς ἑαυτὸν στρεφομένην ᾔσθετο τὴν ἐπιχείρησιν, ἔλεγε πρὸς τοὺς συνήθεις μεγάλην εἶναι τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦ Πλωτίνου δύναμιν, ὡς ἀποκρούειν δύνασθαι τὰς εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐπιφορὰς εἰς τοὺς κακοῦν αὐτὸν ἐπιχειροῦντας. Πλωτῖνος μέντοι τοῦ Ὀλυμπίου ἐγχειροῦντος ἀντελαμβάνετο λέγων αὐτῷ τὸ σῶμα τότε ὡς τὰ σύσπαστα βαλάντια ἕλκεσθαι τῶν μελῶν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἄλληλα συνθλιβομένων. κινδυνεύσας δὲ ὁ Ὀλύμπιος πολλάκις αὐτός τι παθεῖν ἢ δρᾶσαι τὸν Πλωτῖνον ἐπαύσατο.

paragraphs.modern: For Plotinus had something more than others even from birth. An Egyptian priest who had come up to Rome, and had been introduced to him through a friend, wishing to give a proof of his own wisdom, asked Plotinus to come and see the daemon who was with him, his own daemon, as it is called, made visible. Plotinus readily agreed, and the calling up was made in the temple of Isis: that was the only pure place, they say, that the Egyptian could find in Rome. When the daemon was called to show itself, a god came, and not one of the race of daemons; so the Egyptian said: "Blessed are you, for you have a god as your daemon, and the one who is with you is not of the lower race." But they could neither ask it anything nor see it present any longer, because the friend who was watching with them strangled the birds he was holding as a safeguard, whether from envy or from some fear. So, having one of the more divine daemons as his companion, he himself kept raising his own divine eye towards it. It is for this reason that he wrote a book, too, On the daemon allotted to us, where he tries to give the causes of the differences between the companions of each.
paragraphs.greek: ἦν γὰρ καὶ κατὰ γένεσιν πλέον τι ἔχων παρὰ τοὺς ἄλλους ὁ Πλωτῖνος. Αἰγύπτιος γάρ τις ἱερεὺς ἀνελθὼν εἰς τὴν Ῥώμην καὶ διά τινος φίλου αὐτῷ γνωρισθεὶς θέλων τε τῆς ἑαυτοῦ σοφίας ἀπόδειξιν δοῦναι ἠξίωσε τὸν Πλωτῖνον ἐπὶ θέαν ἀφικέσθαι τοῦ συνόντος αὐτῷ οἰκείου δαίμονος καλουμένου. τοῦ δὲ ἑτοίμως ὑπακούσαντος γίνεται μὲν ἐν τῷ Ἰσείῳ ἡ κλῆσις· μόνον γὰρ ἐκεῖνον τὸν τόπον καθαρόν φασιν εὑρεῖν ἐν τῇ Ῥώμῃ τὸν Αἰγύπτιον. κληθέντα δὲ εἰς αὐτοψίαν τὸν δαίμονα θεὸν ἐλθεῖν καὶ μὴ τοῦ δαιμόνων εἶναι γένους· ὅθεν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον εἰπεῖν· μακάριος εἶ θεὸν ἔχων τὸν δαίμονα καὶ οὐ τοῦ ὑφειμένου γένους τὸν συνόντα. μήτε δὲ ἐρέσθαι τι ἐκγενέσθαι μήτε ἐπιπλέον ἰδεῖν παρόντα τοῦ συνθεωροῦντος φίλου τὰς ὄρνεις, ἃς κατεῖχε φυλακῆς ἕνεκα, πνίξαντος εἴτε διὰ φθόνον εἴτε καὶ διὰ φόβον τινά. τῶν οὖν θειοτέρων δαιμόνων ἔχων τὸν συνόντα καὶ αὐτὸς διετέλει ἀνάγων αὐτοῦ τὸ θεῖον ὄμμα πρὸς ἐκεῖνον. ἔστι γοῦν αὐτῷ ἀπὸ τῆς τοιαύτης αἰτίας καὶ βιβλίον γραφὲν περὶ τοῦ εἰληχότος ἡμᾶς δαίμονος, ὅπου πειρᾶται αἰτίας φέρειν περὶ τῆς διαφορᾶς τῶν συνόντων.
notes: The book is III.4. Plato's Timaeus (90a) calls the highest part of the soul the daemon God has given each of us; in the Republic's myth of Er (617e, 620d-e) each soul chooses a life and is given a daemon as its guardian.

paragraphs.modern: When Amelius had become fond of sacrifices, and went round the temples at the new moon and at the feasts, and once asked to take Plotinus with him, Plotinus said: "They must come to me, not I to them." From what thought he spoke so loftily, we could neither understand by ourselves nor did we dare to ask him.
paragraphs.greek: φιλοθύτου δὲ γεγονότος τοῦ Ἀμελίου καὶ τὰ ἱερὰ κατὰ νουμηνίαν καὶ τὰς ἑορτὰς ἐκπεριιόντος καί ποτε ἀξιοῦντος τὸν Πλωτῖνον σὺν αὐτῷ παραλαβεῖν ἔφη· ἐκείνους δεῖ πρὸς ἐμὲ ἔρχεσθαι, οὐκ ἐμὲ πρὸς ἐκείνους. τοῦτο δὲ ἐκ ποίας διανοίας οὕτως ἐμεγαληγόρησεν, οὔτ’ αὐτοὶ συνεῖναι δεδυνήμεθα οὔτ’ αὐτὸν ἐρέσθαι ἐτολμήσαμεν.

paragraphs.modern: He had so great an abundance of insight into character that once, when a costly necklace was stolen from Chione, who lived with him with her children, passing her widowhood with dignity, and the servants were gathered before Plotinus' eyes, he looked at them all and said, "This is the one who stole it," pointing out one of them. The man was whipped, and for a long time at first denied it, but later confessed, brought back what he had stolen and gave it back.
paragraphs.greek: περιῆν δὲ αὐτῷ τοσαύτη περιουσία ἠθῶν κατανοήσεως, ὡς κλοπῆς ποτε γεγονυίας πολυτελοῦς περιδεραίου Χιόνης, ἥτις αὐτῷ συνῴκει μετὰ τῶν τέκνων σεμνῶς τὴν χηρείαν διεξάγουσα, καὶ ὑπ’ ὄψιν τοῦ Πλωτίνου συνηγμένων τῶν οἰκετῶν ἐμβλέψας ἅπασιν· οὗτος, ἔφη, ἐστὶν ὁ κεκλοφώς, δείξας ἕνα τινά. μαστιζόμενος δὲ ἐκεῖνος καὶ ἐπιπλεῖον ἀρνούμενος τὰ πρῶτα ὕστερον ὡμολόγησε καὶ φέρων τὸ κλαπὲν ἀπέδωκε.

paragraphs.modern: He would also foretell, of each of the children who were with him, how he would turn out; so of Polemon, what he would be like: that he would be a lover, given to love, and short-lived, as indeed happened.
paragraphs.greek: προεῖπε δ’ ἂν καὶ τῶν συνόντων παίδων περὶ ἑκάστου οἷος ἀποβήσεται· ὡς καὶ περὶ τοῦ Πολέμωνος οἷος ἔσται, ὅτι ἐρωτικὸς ἔσται καὶ ὀλιγοχρόνιος, ὅπερ καὶ ἀπέβη.

paragraphs.modern: And once he noticed that I, Porphyry, was thinking of taking myself out of life; and he came to me suddenly while I was staying in the house, said that this desire did not come from a state of intellect, but from some melancholic illness, and told me to go away on a journey. I obeyed him and went to Sicily, since I heard that a man of note, Probus, was living near Lilybaeum; and I both gave up that desire and was kept from being with Plotinus until his death.
paragraphs.greek: καί ποτε ἐμοῦ Πορφυρίου ᾔσθετο ἐξάγειν ἐμαυτὸν διανοουμένου τοῦ βίου· καὶ ἐξαίφνης ἐπιστάς μοι ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ διατρίβοντι καὶ εἰπὼν μὴ εἶναι ταύτην τὴν προθυμίαν ἐκ νοερᾶς καταστάσεως, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μελαγχολικῆς τινος νόσου, ἀποδημῆσαι ἐκέλευσε. πεισθεὶς δὲ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ εἰς τὴν Σικελίαν ἀφικόμην Πρόβον τινὰ ἀκούων ἐλλόγιμον ἄνδρα περὶ τὸ Λιλύβαιον διατρίβειν· καὶ αὐτός τε τῆς τοιαύτης προθυμίας ἀπεσχόμην τοῦ τε παρεῖναι ἄχρι θανάτου τῷ Πλωτίνῳ ἐνεποδίσθην.

flags.taylor: to my house where I had secluded myself
flags.why: The Greek says only that Plotinus came to Porphyry "while I was staying in the house" (ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ διατρίβοντι); that he had shut himself away is MacKenna's.

notes: Plotinus' own book On going out of life (I.9, the sixteenth he wrote) teaches that the soul must not be led out of the body by force.

paragraphs.modern: The emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina honoured and revered Plotinus greatly. Making use of their friendship, he asked them to raise up again a city of philosophers that was said to have existed in Campania, but was otherwise in ruins, and to give the country round it to the city once it was settled; those who would live there were to use Plato's laws, and it was to be given the name Platonopolis; and he promised that he would withdraw there himself with his companions. And the philosopher's wish would have come about very easily, had not some of those around the emperor stopped it, from envy, or resentment, or some other wicked cause.
paragraphs.greek: ἐτίμησαν δὲ τὸν Πλωτῖνον μάλιστα καὶ ἐσέφθησαν Γαλιῆνός τε ὁ αὐτοκράτωρ καὶ ἡ τούτου γυνὴ Σαλωνίνα. ὁ δὲ τῇ φιλίᾳ τῇ τούτων καταχρώμενος φιλοσόφων τινὰ πόλιν κατὰ τὴν Καμπανίαν γεγενῆσθαι λεγομένην, ἄλλως δὲ κατηριπωμένην ἠξίου ἀνεγείρειν καὶ τὴν πέριξ χώραν χαρίσασθαι οἰκισθείσῃ τῇ πόλει, νόμοις δὲ χρῆσθαι τοὺς κατοικεῖν μέλλοντας τοῖς Πλάτωνος καὶ τὴν προσηγορίαν αὐτῇ Πλατωνόπολιν θέσθαι, ἐκεῖ τε αὐτὸς μετὰ τῶν ἑταίρων ἀναχωρήσειν ὑπισχνεῖτο. καὶ ἐγένετ’ ἂν τὸ βούλημα ἐκ τοῦ ῥᾴστου τῷ φιλοσόφῳ, εἰ μή τινες τῶν συνόντων τῷ βασιλεῖ φθονοῦντες ἢ νεμεσῶντες ἢ δι’ ἄλλην τινὰ αἰτίαν μοχθηρὰν ἐνεπόδισαν.
notes: Plato's Laws describe the founding of a new city in Crete, Magnesia; the Republic (473c-d) holds that cities will have no rest from evils until philosophers rule.

paragraphs.modern: In the meetings he was able to put things into words, and most powerful at finding and thinking out what fitted the matter; but he made mistakes in some words: he would not say anamimnēsketai ("he recollects") but anamnēmisketai, and other wrongly stamped words, which he kept to in his writing too. When he spoke, the showing of his intellect lit up his face with its light: he was lovely to look at, but then most beautiful to see; a fine sweat ran down him, gentleness shone through him, and he showed kindness towards questions, and vigour.
paragraphs.greek: γέγονε δ’ ἐν ταῖς συνουσίαις φράσαι μὲν ἱκανὸς καὶ εὑρεῖν καὶ νοῆσαι τὰ πρόσφορα δυνατώτατος, ἐν δέ τισι λέξεσιν ἁμαρτάνων· οὐ γὰρ ἂν εἶπεν ἀναμιμνήσκεται, ἀλλ’ ἀναμνημίσκεται, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ παράσημα ὀνόματα, ἃ καὶ ἐν τῷ γράφειν ἐτήρει. ἦν δ’ ἐν τῷ λέγειν ἡ ἔνδειξις τοῦ νοῦ ἄχρι τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ τὸ φῶς ἐπιλάμποντος· ἐράσμιος μὲν ὀφθῆναι, καλλίων δὲ τότε μάλιστα ὁρώμενος· καὶ λεπτός τις ἱδρὼς ἐπέθει καὶ ἡ πρᾳότης διέλαμπε καὶ τὸ προσηνὲς πρὸς τὰς ἐρωτήσεις ἐδείκνυτο καὶ τὸ εὔτονον.

flags.taylor: a slight moisture gathered on his forehead
flags.why: The Greek says only that "a fine sweat ran down" him (λεπτός τις ἱδρὼς ἐπέθει); the forehead is MacKenna's.

flags.taylor: He was always as ready to entertain objections as he was powerful in meeting them
flags.why: The Greek lists what showed in his face as he spoke: his gentleness, his kindness towards questions (τὸ προσηνὲς πρὸς τὰς ἐρωτήσεις) and his vigour (τὸ εὔτονον). MacKenna turns this into a sentence of his own about objections and his power in meeting them.

notes: The two words: ἀναμιμνήσκεται is the right form; Plotinus said ἀναμνημίσκεται, swapping the syllables. Porphyry's point is that the master of thought was no master of grammar.

paragraphs.modern: For three days, for example, when I, Porphyry, asked him how the soul is present with the body, he kept on demonstrating, so that when a man named Thaumasius came in, who dealt in general discourses and said that he wanted to hear him speak in a way fit for books, and could not bear Porphyry answering and asking, Plotinus said: "But if we do not solve the difficulties when Porphyry asks, we shall not be able to say anything at all for the book."
paragraphs.greek: τριῶν γοῦν ἡμερῶν ἐμοῦ Πορφυρίου ἐρωτήσαντος, πῶς ἡ ψυχὴ σύνεστι τῷ σώματι, παρέτεινεν ἀποδεικνύς, ὥστε καὶ Θαυμασίου τινὸς τοὔνομα ἐπεισελθόντος τοὺς καθόλου λόγους πράττοντος καὶ εἰς βιβλία ἀκοῦσαι αὐτοῦ λέγοντος θέλειν, Πορφυρίου δὲ ἀποκρινομένου καὶ ἐρωτῶντος μὴ ἀνέχεσθαι, ἔφη· ἀλλὰ ἂν μὴ Πορφυρίου ἐρωτῶντος λύσωμεν τὰς ἀπορίας, εἰπεῖν τι καθάπαξ εἰς τὸ βιβλίον οὐ δυνησόμεθα.

flags.taylor: a man called Thomasius
flags.why: The Greek name is Θαυμάσιος, Thaumasius.

notes: Volkmann reads ἀποκρινομένου, "answering"; the modern version keeps it. The question how the soul is present with the body is the subject of Plotinus' IV.3, the first of the books On difficulties about the soul (done beside Taylor).

paragraphs.modern: In writing he was concise and full of thought, brief, and richer in ideas than in words, mostly speaking with inspiration and passion. Mixed into his writings, though hidden, are the doctrines of the Stoics and the Peripatetics; and Aristotle's Metaphysics too is packed into them. No theorem, as they call it, of geometry escaped him, nor of arithmetic, nor of mechanics, optics or musical theory; but he was not set on working these out himself.
paragraphs.greek: ἐν δὲ τῷ γράφειν σύντομος γέγονε καὶ πολύνους βραχύς τε καὶ νοήμασι πλεονάζων ἢ λέξεσι, τὰ πολλὰ ἐνθουσιῶν καὶ ἐκπαθῶς φράζων. ἐμμέμικται δ’ ἐν τοῖς συγγράμμασι καὶ τὰ Στωικὰ λανθάνοντα δόγματα καὶ τὰ Περιπατητικά· καταπεπύκνωται δὲ καὶ ἡ μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ τοῦ Ἀριστοτέλους πραγματεία. ἔλαθε δὲ αὐτὸν οὔτε γεωμετρικόν τι λεγόμενον θεώρημα οὔτ’ ἀριθμητικόν, οὐ μηχανικόν, οὐκ ὀπτικόν, οὐ μουσικόν· αὐτὸς δὲ ταῦτα ἐξεργάζεσθαι οὐ παρεσκεύαστο.

flags.taylor: He followed his own path rather than that of tradition
flags.why: There is nothing for this in Volkmann's Greek, which goes straight from "speaking with inspiration and passion" to the Stoic and Peripatetic doctrines.

flags.taylor: is condensed in them, all but entire
flags.why: The Greek says only that the Metaphysics "is packed into" his writings too (καταπεπύκνωται); "all but entire" is MacKenna's.

flags.taylor: Geometry, Mechanics, Optics and Music
flags.why: MacKenna leaves out arithmetic (ἀριθμητικόν), which the Greek names after geometry.

notes: "The Peripatetics" are Aristotle's school. Plotinus' VI.1 to VI.3, On the kinds of being, examine Aristotle's categories and the Stoics' at length.

paragraphs.modern: In the meetings the commentaries were read out to him: they might be by Severus, or Cronius, or Numenius, or Gaius, or Atticus, and among the Peripatetics by Aspasius, Alexander, Adrastus and any that came to hand. But nothing was simply said from them: he was original and different in his study, and brought the intellect of Ammonius to his inquiries. He took the matter in quickly, and after giving the sense of a deep theorem in a few words, he would rise. When Longinus' On principles and his Lover of antiquity were read to him, he said: "Longinus is a scholar, but not a philosopher at all."
paragraphs.greek: ἐν δὲ ταῖς συνουσίαις ἀνεγινώσκετο μὲν αὐτῷ τὰ ὑπομνήματα, εἴτε Σεβήρου εἴη, εἴτε Κρονίου ἢ Νουμηνίου ἢ Γαίου ἢ Ἀττικοῦ, κἀν τοῖς Περιπατητικοῖς τά τε Ἀσπασίου καὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου Ἀδράστου τε καὶ τῶν ἐμπεσόντων. ἐλέγετο δὲ ἐκ τούτων οὐδὲν καθάπαξ, ἀλλ’ ἴδιος ἦν καὶ ἐξηλλαγμένος ἐν τῇ θεωρίᾳ καὶ τὸν Ἀμμωνίου φέρων νοῦν ἐν ταῖς ἐξετάσεσιν. ἐπληροῦτο δὲ ταχέως καὶ δι’ ὀλίγων δοὺς νοῦν βαθέος θεωρήματος ἀνίστατο. ἀναγνωσθέντος δὲ αὐτῷ τοῦ τε περὶ ἀρχῶν Λογγίνου καὶ τοῦ φιλαρχαίου ‘φιλόλογος μέν’, ἔφη, ‘ὁ Λογγῖνος, φιλόσοφος δὲ οὐδαμῶς.’

flags.taylor: Longinus' work On Causes
flags.why: The title is περὶ ἀρχῶν, On principles (or "On first principles"), not "On causes".

flags.taylor: a few words sufficed him to make clear the significance of some profound theory and so to pass on
flags.why: The Greek ἀνίστατο is "he rose": having given the sense in a few words, he stood up and ended the meeting.

notes: Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius and Atticus are Platonists of the second century; Aspasius, Alexander (of Aphrodisias) and Adrastus are commentators on Aristotle. Longinus, the critic and scholar who taught Porphyry at Athens, appears again in chapters 19 to 21. "Lover of antiquity" (φιλάρχαιος) is the title of one of his books.

paragraphs.modern: Once when Origen came to the meeting, Plotinus went red and wanted to rise; and when Origen asked him to speak, he said that one's eagerness flags when the speaker knows that he is speaking to people who already know what he is going to say; and so, after talking a little, he got up and left.
paragraphs.greek: Ὠριγένους δὲ ἀπαντήσαντός ποτε εἰς τὴν συνουσίαν πληρωθεὶς ἐρυθήματος ἀνίστασθαι μὲν ἐβούλετο, λέγειν δὲ ὑπὸ Ὠριγένους ἀξιούμενος ἔφη ἀνίλλεσθαι τὰς προθυμίας, ὅταν εἰδῇ ὁ λέγων, ὅτι πρὸς εἰδότας ἐρεῖ, ἃ αὐτὸς μέλλει λέγειν· καὶ οὕτως ὀλίγα διαλεχθεὶς ἐξανέστη.
notes: This Origen is the Platonist, Plotinus' fellow pupil under Ammonius (chapter 3).

paragraphs.modern: When at Plato's feast I read a poem, The sacred marriage, and someone said that Porphyry was mad, because much of it was said in the language of the mysteries, with inspiration and in a hidden way, Plotinus said so that all could hear: "You have shown yourself at once poet, philosopher and hierophant."
paragraphs.greek: ἐμοῦ δὲ ἐν Πλατωνείοις ποίημα ἀναγνόντος τὸν ἱερὸν γάμον, καί τινος διὰ τὸ μυστικῶς πολλὰ μετ’ ἐνθουσιασμοῦ ἐπικεκρυμμένως εἰρῆσθαι εἰπόντος μαίνεσθαι τὸν Πορφύριον, ἐκεῖνος εἰς ἐπήκοον ἔφη πάντων· ‘ἔδειξας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ τὸν φιλόσοφον καὶ τὸν ἱεροφάντην.’
notes: "Plato's feast" (Πλατώνεια) is the feast Plotinus gave on Plato's birthday (chapter 2). The hierophant is the priest who shows the sacred things at the Mysteries of Eleusis.

paragraphs.modern: When the orator Diophanes read a defence of Alcibiades in Plato's Symposium, laying it down that for the sake of learning virtue a pupil must give himself to a teacher who desires him, even for sexual union, Plotinus several times leapt up to leave the gathering, but held himself back; and after the audience broke up he told me, Porphyry, to write a reply. Since Diophanes would not give me the book, I recalled his arguments from memory, wrote the reply, and read it before the same hearers gathered again, and I pleased Plotinus so much that at the meetings he kept saying: "Shoot like that, and you may become a light to men."
paragraphs.greek: ὅτε δὲ ὁ ῥήτωρ Διοφάνης ἀνέγνω ὑπὲρ Ἀλκιβιάδου τοῦ ἐν τῷ Συμποσίῳ τοῦ Πλάτωνος ἀπολογίαν δογματίζων χρῆναι ἀρετῆς ἕνεκα μαθήσεως εἰς συνουσίαν αὐτὸν παρέχειν ἐρῶντι ἀφροδισίου μίξεως τῷ καθηγεμόνι, ἤιξε μὲν πολλάκις ἀναστὰς ἀπαλλαγῆναι τῆς συνόδου, ἐπισχὼν δ’ ἑαυτὸν μετὰ τὴν διάλυσιν τοῦ ἀκουστηρίου ἐμοὶ Πορφυρίῳ ἀντιγράψαι προσέταξε. μὴ θέλοντος δὲ τοῦ Διοφάνους τὸ βιβλίον δοῦναι διὰ τῆς μνήμης ἀναληφθέντων τῶν ἐπιχειρημάτων ἀντιγράψας ἐγὼ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν αὐτῶν ἀκροατῶν συνηγμένων ἀναγνοὺς τοσοῦτον τὸν Πλωτῖνον ηὔφρανα, ὡς κἀν ταῖς συνουσίαις συνεχῶς ἐπιλέγειν· βάλλ’ οὕτως, αἴ κέν τι φόως ἄνδρεσσι γένηαι.

flags.taylor: should submit to the teacher without reserve
flags.why: The Greek says the pupil should give himself "to the teacher who desires him" (ἐρῶντι ... τῷ καθηγεμόνι); "without reserve" is MacKenna's, and he leaves out the teacher's desire.

flags.taylor: during the very reading he repeatedly quoted
flags.why: The Greek says that Plotinus "kept saying it at the meetings" (κἀν ταῖς συνουσίαις συνεχῶς ἐπιλέγειν), afterwards and often, not during the reading.

notes: In the Symposium (217a-219d) Alcibiades tells how he offered himself to Socrates in exchange for his wisdom, and was refused. Plotinus' line is Homer's Iliad 8.282, Agamemnon to the archer Teucer ("shoot like that, and you may become a light to the Danaans"), with "men" for "Danaans".

paragraphs.modern: When Eubulus, the Platonic successor, wrote from Athens and sent writings on some Platonic questions, Plotinus had them given to me, Porphyry, and asked me to examine them and report to him what was written. He paid attention to the tables of the stars, though not at all as a mathematician, but to the forecasts of the casters of nativities more closely; and having caught out how little their promise could be trusted, he did not hesitate to refute it in many places in his writings too.
paragraphs.greek: γράφοντος δὲ Εὐβούλου Ἀθήνηθεν τοῦ Πλατωνικοῦ διαδόχου καὶ πέμποντος συγγράμματα ὑπέρ τινων Πλατωνικῶν ζητημάτων ἐμοὶ Πορφυρίῳ ταῦτα δίδοσθαι ἐποίει καὶ σκοπεῖν καὶ ἀναφέρειν αὐτῷ τὰ γεγραμμένα ἠξίου. προσεῖχε δὲ τοῖς μὲν περὶ τῶν ἀστέρων κανόσιν οὐ πάνυ τι μαθηματικῶς, τοῖς δὲ τῶν γενεθλιαλόγων ἀποτελεστικοῖς ἀκριβέστερον. καὶ φωράσας τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τὸ ἀνεχέγγυον ἐλέγχειν πολλαχοῦ καὶ ἐν τοῖς συγγράμμασιν οὐκ ὤκνησε.

flags.taylor: the principles of Astronomy
flags.why: The Greek κανόνες are "tables" (the astronomers' tables of the stars' movements), used to cast nativities; it is these that Plotinus studied "not at all as a mathematician".

notes: The "successor" (διάδοχος) is the head of the Platonic school at Athens, Plato's successor. Plotinus refutes the astrologers in II.3, Whether the stars are causes, and III.1, On destiny.

paragraphs.modern: In his time there were many others, Christians, and among them sectarians who had set out from the ancient philosophy, the followers of Adelphius and Aquilinus, who owned a great many writings of Alexander the Libyan, Philocomus and Demostratus the Lydian, and brought out revelations of Zoroaster, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Mesus and others of that kind; they deceived many, and were deceived themselves, saying that Plato had not come near the depth of intelligible being.
paragraphs.greek: γεγόνασι δὲ κατ’ αὐτὸν τῶν Χριστιανῶν πολλοὶ μὲν καὶ ἄλλοι, αἱρετικοὶ δὲ ἐκ τῆς παλαιᾶς φιλοσοφίας ἀνηγμένοι οἱ περὶ Ἀδέλφιον καὶ Ἀκυλῖνον, οἳ τὰ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Λίβυος καὶ Φιλοκώμου καὶ Δημοστράτου τοῦ Λυδοῦ συγγράμματα πλεῖστα κεκτημένοι ἀποκαλύψεις τε προφέροντες Ζωροάστρου καὶ Ζωστριανοῦ καὶ Νικοθέου καὶ Ἀλλογενοῦς καὶ Μέσου καὶ ἄλλων τοιούτων πολλοὺς ἐξηπάτων καὶ αὐτοὶ ἠπατημένοι, ὡς δὴ τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰς τὸ βάθος τῆς νοητῆς οὐσίας οὐ πελάσαντος.

flags.taylor: works by Alexander of Lydia, by Philocomus, by Demostratus and by Lydus
flags.why: Volkmann's Greek reads "Alexander the Libyan" (τοῦ Λίβυος) and "Demostratus the Lydian" (τοῦ Λυδοῦ): MacKenna makes Alexander a Lydian, and the Lydian a fourth author, "Lydus".

notes: The Greek can also be read "many Christians, and others": the sentence has been taken both ways. The sectarians (αἱρετικοί) are those whom Plotinus' book calls Gnostics.
A modern finding, not in Porphyry: books called Zostrianus and Allogenes survive in Coptic, among the manuscripts found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945.

paragraphs.modern: So he himself made many refutations at the meetings, and also wrote the book which we have titled Against the Gnostics, and left the rest to us to judge. Amelius went on as far as forty books writing against the book of Zostrianus; and I, Porphyry, have made many refutations of the book of Zoroaster, showing that the book is spurious and recent, made up by those who founded the sect, so that it would be thought that the doctrines they had chosen to honour were those of the ancient Zoroaster.
paragraphs.greek: ὅθεν αὐτὸς μὲν πολλοὺς ἐλέγχους ποιούμενος ἐν ταῖς συνουσίαις, γράψας δὲ καὶ βιβλίον, ὅπερ πρὸς τοὺς Γνωστικοὺς ἐπεγράψαμεν, ἡμῖν τὰ λοιπὰ κρίνειν καταλέλοιπεν. Ἀμέλιος δὲ ἄχρι τεσσαράκοντα βιβλίων προκεχώρηκε πρὸς τὸ Ζωστριανοῦ βιβλίον ἀντιγράφων. Πορφύριος δὲ ἐγὼ πρὸς τὸ Ζωροάστρου συχνοὺς πεποίημαι ἐλέγχους, (ὅπως) νόθον τε καὶ νέον τὸ βιβλίον παραδεικνὺς πεπλασμένον τε ὑπὸ τῶν τὴν αἵρεσιν συστησαμένων εἰς δόξαν τοῦ εἶναι τοῦ παλαιοῦ Ζωροάστρου τὰ δόγματα, ἃ αὐτοὶ εἵλοντο πρεσβεύειν.
notes: Against the Gnostics is II.9 (the thirty-third book by date), done beside Taylor. Volkmann sets ὅπως, "so that", in round brackets.

paragraphs.modern: Since people in Greece were saying that he was passing off Numenius' work as his own, and Trypho, the Stoic and Platonist, reported this to Amelius, Amelius wrote a book which he titled On the difference between the doctrines of Plotinus and Numenius, and dedicated it to me, as Basileus. Basileus was the name I, Porphyry, had: in my native tongue I was called Malchus, which was my father's name too, and Malchus means basileus ("king") if one wants to turn it into Greek. So Longinus, dedicating his On impulse to Cleodamus and to me, Porphyry, wrote at its head "Cleodamus and Malchus"; and Amelius, translating the name, as Numenius turned Maximus into Megalos, writes Basileus for Malchus:
paragraphs.greek: τῶν δ’ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἑλλάδος τὰ Νουμηνίου αὐτὸν ὑποβάλλεσθαι λεγόντων καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς Ἀμέλιον ἀγγέλλοντος Τρύφωνος τοῦ Στωικοῦ τε καὶ Πλατωνικοῦ γέγραφεν ὁ Ἀμέλιος βιβλίον, ὃ ἐπέγραψε μὲν περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὰ δόγματα τοῦ Πλωτίνου πρὸς τὸν Νουμήνιον διαφορᾶς, προσεφώνησε δὲ αὐτὸ Βασιλεῖ ἐμοί· Βασιλεὺς δὲ τοὔνομα τῷ Πορφυρίῳ ἐμοὶ προσῆν, κατὰ μὲν πάτριον διάλεκτον Μάλχῳ κεκλημένῳ, ὅπερ μοι καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὄνομα κέκλητο, τοῦ δὲ Μάλχου ἑρμηνείαν ἔχοντος βασιλεύς, εἴ τις εἰς Ἑλληνίδα διάλεκτον μεταβάλλειν ἐθέλοι. ὅθεν ὁ Λογγῖνος μὲν προσφωνῶν τὰ περὶ ὁρμῆς Κλεοδάμῳ τε κἀμοὶ Πορφυρίῳ ‘Κλεόδαμέ τε καὶ Μάλχε’ προὔγραψεν· ὁ δ’ Ἀμέλιος ἑρμηνεύσας τοὔνομα, ὡς ὁ Νουμήνιος τὸν Μάξιμον εἰς τὸν Μέγαλον, οὕτως τὸν Μάλχον οὗτος εἰς τὸν Βασιλέα γράφει· ‘

flags.taylor: it is equivalent to Porphyry (Purple-robed)
flags.why: Not in the Greek: Porphyry says only that Malchus, his native name, means "king". That "Porphyry" ("purple") also suits a king is MacKenna's addition.

notes: Porphyry was from Tyre, in Phoenicia; malk is "king" in the Semitic languages spoken there. Maximus is Latin for "greatest", Megalos Greek for "great".

paragraphs.modern: "Amelius to Basileus, greetings. For the sake of those highly praised men themselves who, as you say, have dinned into your ears that our companion's doctrines go back to Numenius of Apamea, I would never have let out a word, you may be sure. For plainly this too comes from the fine speech and fluency they pride themselves on: saying now that he is a great babbler, now that he is a plagiarist, and thirdly that what he passes off as his own is the poorest stuff there is, plainly to mock him when they speak against him.
paragraphs.greek: Ἀμέλιος Βασιλεῖ εὖ πράττειν. Αὐτῶν μὲν ἕνεκα τῶν πανευφήμων ἀνδρῶν, οὓς διατεθρυλληκέναι σεαυτὸν φής, τὰ τοῦ ἑταίρου ἡμῶν δόγματα εἰς τὸν Ἀπαμέα Νουμήνιον ἀναγόντων, οὐκ ἂν προηκάμην φωνήν, σαφῶς ἐπίστασο. δῆλον γάρ, ὅτι καὶ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἀγαλλομένης προελήλυθεν εὐστομίας τε καὶ εὐγλωττίας, νῦν μὲν ὅτι πλατὺς φλήναφος, αὖθις δὲ ὅτι ὑποβολιμαῖος, ἐκ τρίτων δὲ ὅτι καὶ τὰ φαυλότατα τῶν ὄντων ὑποβαλλόμενος τῷ διασιλλαίνειν αὐτὸν δηλαδὴ κατ’ αὐτοῦ λεγόντων.

flags.taylor: he bases the universe on the meanest of existents
flags.why: The Greek ὑποβαλλόμενος is the same word as in "passing off" Numenius' work: the third charge is most naturally that what he passes off is the poorest of things. MacKenna reads it as "putting under", a foundation for the universe.
